title: The Impact of AI on Educational Assessment: A Framework for Constructive Alignment
extended_summary:
This paper examines how the growing use of artificial intelligence, especially large language models, affects the validity of educational assessment. The central questions are whether AI changes whether an assessment remains valid and how that influence differs across learning objectives at different Bloom’s taxonomy levels. The paper argues that the presence of AI creates new challenges for aligning learning objectives and assessment, especially when students may use AI tools in formative or summative tasks.

The main approach is a theoretical framework built from Constructive Alignment and Bloom’s taxonomy, combined with a small empirical survey of university course coordinators. The framework proposes that AI should generally be forbidden in assessment for lower-level objectives such as Remember and Understand, because AI use would undermine measurement of students’ own recall and comprehension. For higher Bloom levels such as Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create, the paper proposes a more nuanced approach in which course coordinators decide among different levels of permissible AI use for distinct assessment components. It also argues that formative and summative assessment should be aligned in whether AI is allowed.

The empirical component is a survey of 24 course coordinators at TU Delft, with responses covering bachelor’s, master’s, and one doctoral course. Most responses concerned take-home assignments. The context is higher education in the Netherlands, focused on instructors’ perceptions of AI in assessment rather than direct measurement of student learning outcomes. The survey explored lecturers’ attitudes toward AI, the Bloom levels of their course objectives, desired levels of AI use in assignments, and perceived difficulty of enforcing AI restrictions.

The paper concludes that assessment methods should be redesigned to account for AI, with careful alignment between learning objectives, assessment format, and AI policy. It finds that lecturers generally agree AI requires adaptation of education and assessment, but their preferences are biased by their own familiarity and use of AI. The author recommends clearer institutional guidelines, explicit communication to students about permitted AI use, and training for teaching staff on AI capabilities and limitations. The paper also notes that its findings should be interpreted cautiously because they rely on lecturers’ self-assessments and require further validation using student and expert perspectives.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's large language model chatbot for generating and transforming text.
identified_tools.use_case: Discussed as the prominent example of generative AI/LLM tools driving concerns about the validity of educational assessment and motivating a constructive alignment framework; not empirically evaluated as an intervention on student outcomes.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic generative AI and large language model tools used for text generation, summarization, paraphrasing, feedback, and related language tasks.
identified_tools.use_case: Used as the conceptual tool category in a theoretical framework on how AI affects assessment validity across Bloom levels and in a lecturer survey about permitted AI use in assessment.

quality_tier_rationale: The paper presents a theoretical framework plus a small lecturer survey (24 complete responses), but it does not evaluate an AI tool's causal effect on student learning outcomes. Evidence is primarily conceptual and perception-based rather than experimental.
impact_tier_rationale: No direct student outcome effects or effect sizes are reported for any AI tool. The paper suggests potentially important implications for assessment policy and practice, but empirical impact remains unclear.
